title: Trust narratives for degradation
body:
Purpose:
This is a working brief for GTM and Customer Success to standardize how we talk about degraded behavior, fallbacks, and multi-region failovers. Goal: give field teams clear language and templates to build customer trust quickly while minimizing technical jargon and legal exposure.

Audience:
- Engineering-forward PMs and SREs evaluating inference resiliency
- Platform/infra buyers at startups and mid-market SaaS
- Internal CS/AM responding to incidents

Elevator (one-liner to use in pitches):
Redwood keeps your product online during model or region-level degradation by routing to compatible variants and regions with predictable cost/latency trade-offs — and we tell you exactly what changed and why.

Core positioning pillars (short statements to repeat):
1) Predictable degradation: Your app degrades in measurable, policy-driven ways rather than failing silently.
2) Safe fallbacks: When primary capacity is constrained we automatically route requests to compatible model variants or alternate regions with explicit SLOs per tier.
3) Transparent comms: We log and surface what degraded, why, and how it affected output quality so you can make product-level decisions.
4) Choice and control: You define the fallback hierarchy — prefer lower-cost or lower-latency options — and we enforce it.

Tone & trust language guide:
- Use active reassurance: "We routed traffic to a verified backup model to keep your feature responsive."
- Avoid absolutes or over-promises: prefer "aim to" / "target" / "our current SLOs" rather than "always".
- Name the visible customer impact first, then the technical cause at a high level.
- Call out mitigation and next steps (what we fixed, how we prevent recurrence) within the first message window.
- Use plain comparisons, not technical deep-dives, for non-engineering audiences.

Incident narrative templates (short, medium, long formats):
1) Proactive heads-up (pre-failure, when we change routing policies or run a risky rollout):
  Subject: Upcoming routing test — potential minor latency changes in eu-west1
  Body: We will be testing a new cross-region routing rule on DATE. This may cause a small percentage of EU traffic to be routed to our eu-north config, which can increase median latency by ~30ms for some requests. No customer action required. If you prefer to opt-out, here's a link to change your fallback policy.

2) Tier 1 incident (transient capacity shortage; low customer impact):
  Short: We detected high GPU contention that affected a subset of requests. We routed affected calls to a verified model variant and region to keep responses streaming. You may see slightly shorter responses or increased latency for 8–15 minutes.
  Medium: Explain cause: burst in demand in region X -> autoscaler delay. Mitigation: activated tiered routing and added capacity; CS will follow up with logs and a postmortem link within 72 hours.

3) Tier 2 incident (sustained degraded outputs / quality regression):
  Short: We observed degraded output quality from the primary model for a subset of prompts. As a precaution we automatically switched to a model variant with equivalent safety profiles and stronger QA for the affected prompts. We’re investigating the regression and will share findings and any customer-relevant remediation steps.
  Template phrases: "We prioritized correctness over latency for impacted traffic to avoid incorrect outputs." "We have frozen rollouts for the model and rolled back to the previous version."

Fallback messaging — examples and rules:
- Multi-region fallback (customer-facing):
  "If Redwood detects regional capacity constraints, your requests are routed to the nearest healthy region that meets your latency policy. You can choose stricter routing to limit cross-region traffic (control plane setting: region.strictness)."
- Model-variant fallback (developer-facing):
  "Fallbacks follow this hierarchy: pinned model version -> compatible quantized variant -> cheaper high-throughput variant -> cross-region equivalent. Each step includes automatic prefix/KV cache reconciliation to minimize state drift."
- Value guidance: Clearly call out the trade-off (latency vs cost vs output fidelity). Give examples: "Routing to region B reduces success rate for image-to-caption prompts by ~5% in our test prompts."

Customer-facing templates (two short examples):
1) Reactive — brief email:
  Subject: Quick update: degraded inference in us-west; feature remained online
  Body: We detected capacity pressure in us-west today at 10:12 PDT. To avoid outages, we routed affected calls to a verified backup fleet in us-east; feature remained online but median latency increased from 120ms to 210ms for ~2% of requests between 10:12–10:28. No customer data was exposed. Postmortem: LINK (72h).

2) Proactive — product change:
  Subject: New fallback control for latency-sensitive routes
  Body: You can now opt into strict-local routing per route to guarantee sub-100ms targeting. This may increase error rates during region-wide capacity events. How to enable: LINK.

Competitive differentiation notes (short bullets for rebuttals):
- Generic cloud LLM endpoints: Often default to cold failures under peak due to single-region autoscaling limits. We emphasize policy-driven graceful degradation and verified model-variants to remain online.
- Pure self-hosted runtimes: Provide control but shift all operational risk to the customer. Redwood provides managed fallbacks + audit trails so you don’t have to build the fallback logic yourself.
- Other inference platforms: Some provide multi-region routing; few surface customer-facing explanations, trade-offs, and post-incident quality sign-offs in the same console.

Proof points and metrics to cite (what to show customers):
- % of incidents where routing prevented total outage (example stat: "Routing prevented >99% of feature outages in last 12 months").
- Average additional latency introduced by multi-region fallback (median & p95 by region).
- Measured quality delta for each fallback model variant on representative eval set.
- Audit logs: number of routed requests, reason code tags, and token-level cost deltas.

Demo & sales kit ideas:
- Live demo: induce a controlled capacity constraint in a sandbox and show automatic routing + console explanations and trace link.
- One-pager: "How your app behaves during an availability event" with visual flowchart.
- CS playbook: checklist for what to say in first 10 minutes / 1 hour / 24 hours.

Open questions for product/legal/engineering:
- How granular should default routing policies be? per-route, per-tenant, or per-model?
- What standard language does Legal want for "no data exposure" statements in reactive emails?
- Can engineering expose an SLO ladder for each fallback step (e.g., fallbacks only used to meet availability SLOs, not accuracy SLOs)?

Next steps (action items):
- GTM to try templates in two upcoming customer incidents and gather feedback.
- Product to define default fallback policies and CLI/console toggles (deadline: end of Q2).
- Metrics: SRE to produce quarterly "availability-with-fallbacks" metric for sales decks.

Notes: This doc is a working draft — keep language short and measurable, prefer concrete examples over abstract claims. Add copies of actual customer incident emails here once approved for reuse.
